newsitem.title: UK: LME trade unexciting, copper works upwards by close.
newsitem.headline: LME trade unexciting, copper works upwards by close.

text.p: Base metal trading on the LME remained fairly humdrum during Tuesday afternoon, and although prices moved up from early lows there was little substance in movements.

Traders said copper led the way, but again lost impetus at the $2,380 level, while nickel fluctuated wildly, but was always in the minus column, due to rising inventories and less concern over Russian supply disruption.
"It has been slow all day, really. Even copper was basically ranging - we only saw a move towards the end of the day," one floor trader said.

The tone was set in copper after a 4,300-tonne inventory fall, which was due to 3,125 tonnes moving out of the Singapore warehouse for China. But the stock fall there was anticipated, and further short-term declines are likely to meet arbitrage shipments to China. Physical premiums for Singapore are rising, traders said.

LME prices made little real headway, with prices some way off the upper and lower ends of the current range. Consequently, volume was thin. There was more interest this afternoon, but stops were not hit above $2,380, and last kerb trade was at $2,377, up $10 a tonne from Monday.
Nickel trading was volatile, with the market showing its usual unpredictability in the face of fundamental developments, although the trend was generally lower.
Losses were initially induced by the 846-tonne increase in stocks before the market perversely rallied away from lows under $7,700, despite news that Norilsk workers had decided not to halt output.

Traders said a snap $100 bounce, which was at odds with cash selling in the official rings, reflected fund buying and trader covering. Afternoon business was less erratic, and prices dipped under $7,800 once more to end at $7,780, down $40 from Monday.

Aluminium turned away from its lows during the afternoon, but remained softer following a morning sell-off. Traders said the rally back above $1,650 lacked conviction, and final business was at $1,653, down $4.
Zinc also reversed direction during the afternoon, with price dips seen as buying opportunities at present, while another inventory trend was also indicative of solid fundamentals.
Interest picked up during the kerb, when there was another foray above $1,300, although three months ended at $1,299, up $5 from the previous close
Lead recovered from a midsession sell-off by Chinese operators, but the pace of trading was slow, matching dull physicals, and by the end of the kerb prices were still unchanged at $679 a tonne.

Tin sentiment took a knock from the 700-tonne rise in stocks, which followed a sizeable increase last Friday. The short-lived backwardation of last week has attracted some 1,100 tonnes of metal to the market, with total stocks now at 10,205 tonnes.
Prices held above the lows during late trading, helped by copper's snap up, but last kerb trade at $5,845 was still down $25.
Alloy was quiet, but closed at a stable $1,545/55 a tonne.
